prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought atomic frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 1e-18 and opened new tests of relativity and fundamental constants

statement.case_for: After the full round-1 exchange I keep B042 as a single-achievement prize to Katori and Ye, and I hold it with more confidence than before. The evidence I weigh most is independent confirmation, and here it is plain: 1e-18 class performance has been reproduced and cross-compared at JILA/NIST, RIKEN and Tokyo, SYRTE and PTB. Seven of eight members ranked it at the opening, and four now prefer it. Both of the others who prefer B019 (Eriksson, Olsson) name it as their first alternative, and Mehlig does so too, so it is the one configuration that nobody in the room regards as a poor outcome. On the science, the magic-wavelength condition is one clean physical criterion that cancels the dominant light shift for thousands of atoms at once. Getting from that idea to 1e-18 required real understanding of blackbody, collisional and tunnelling shifts and of laser coherence, which is detector-building of the kind I respect. The consequences are already physical results: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter limits on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings. Attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist. Katori supplied the concept and first demonstration and Ye drove the instrument to record accuracy and stability, and every member who proposed laureates named the same two people.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised by Olsson, Mehlig and in part Eriksson, is that this is a refinement of a measurement line already honoured in 2005 (combs) and 2012 (ion control), and that Ye's clocks are partly later and better execution of Katori's idea. A second objection is priority: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley and Bloom were decisive in particular demonstrations and a two-name prize cannot cover them, though this is true of nearly every candidate and is not specific to this one. Third, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so some will say wait. I think the redefinition is irrelevant to a physics prize, since it is a metrological decision, and I would keep it out of the citation. Finally, the room has a legitimate concern about a further AMO prize after 2005, 2012, 2022, 2023 and 2025. I do not treat that as disqualifying, but it is a real appetite question and not a scientific one.

responses.point: Olsson asks what Ye's clocks add that is original rather than merely superior, and treats Katori as the original contribution.
responses.response: That is the right question and I will answer it directly. What Ye's group added is not only a smaller number. Reaching 1e-18 meant characterising and suppressing the blackbody shift, controlling collisional and tunnelling effects with spin-polarised many-atom interrogation, and demonstrating laser coherence long enough to use the atoms. These were new physical understanding and are what made the Katori idea a working quantum-limited oscillator. I would therefore word the citation around the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, with no reference to combs. If you still read Ye as execution only, then the committee's choice is whether to credit Katori alone, and I do not think a one-name prize is defensible when the record-accuracy realisation was done at JILA and was reproduced in Tokyo, Paris and Braunschweig.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B019 but says he would support B042 if the committee judges twisted bilayer graphene too young, and asks whether Ye's comb and cavity work is separable from the 2005 prize.
responses.response: Thank you for the clear fall-back. On separability, yes: the comb is a ruler the clock reads out, and the 2005 prize rewarded it. The magic-wavelength lattice, the many-atom interrogation and the ultrastable cavity are different contributions, and I will propose wording that leaves the comb out. On B019 I am not hostile. Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by the 2018 experiments is the best prediction-then-discovery story on the list. But you and Olsson both concede that the pairing mechanism is open and that the first author and student team cannot be named, and you ask whether eight years is enough. My own test is independent confirmation of a settled result, and for the phases it is met, but for the physical interpretation it is not. I would keep B019 as my first alternative and would want it considered again in a few years.

responses.point: Kroll says IceCube is the best non-AMO competitor if Halzen and Spiering cover the decisive credit, but ranks it behind the clocks on interpretive maturity and notes pioneer problems with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND.
responses.response: I accept that critique of my own opening favourite, and it has moved me. The diffuse flux is secure but the source identifications are still at 3 to 4 sigma, and from my own cosmic-ray background I know how much a new window changes in its first decade. I cannot say that Spiering's Baikal and DUMAND-era role is as decisive as Halzen's relative to the other pioneers, and a two-name prize would leave out people I would be uncomfortable omitting. That is why I now list B019 ahead of B032 among my alternatives. Separately, I note your disclosure of a year in John Hall's laboratory. I do not see it as a recusal-level tie to Katori or Ye, since Hall's prize was for combs and no collaboration is reported, but it should stay on the record.

responses.point: Mehlig weighs the clocks nearer to engineering refinement and values a simple, general mechanism, and ranked them only seventh.
responses.response: Your criterion is one I can meet on this candidate: the magic-wavelength condition is a single simple criterion that removes the dominant systematic, and it carries over to different species and geometries, which is the generality you value in twisted bilayers. Where we differ is on whether a measured discovery needs a new object, and I would say a regime of measurement that resolves a millimetre of gravitational redshift is a result about nature. I note your move from KPZ to B019 and I do not argue that you are wrong to rank a new phase of matter above a measurement capability, which is a judgement of taste the committee has to make openly. I ask only that your fall-back be B042 and not B037, as you indicated.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from the Higgs experiments to IceCube and prefers a new window on nature to a refinement.
responses.response: I understand the preference, and it was mine at the opening. I would put to you that the lattice clock is also a new window: a clock that can see a height difference of a millimetre is a new gravitational and dark-matter sensor, and that is the use I would stress. On B032 I cannot yet answer your claim that the 2002 prize is no obstacle. I raised it as a question, I think the diffuse flux alone is a fair basis for a citation, and I would not oppose B032 as a later prize once sources pass 5 sigma. For B057 you have heard Olsson and me say the credited three are detector leaders, so I still need an answer on which of them is weakest and whether a detector-centred citation would satisfy you.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto or others have a priority claim that would change the pair; I rely on the ballots and my memory for exact order of the first strontium lattice demonstrations.
Whether the committee reads lattice clocks as a discovery about nature or as an instrument advance after 2005 and 2012; I judge it sufficient but this is a matter of committee taste.
Whether awarding Ye now complicates a later case for the thorium nuclear clock, which is not on the shortlist.
For B019, what in the pairing mechanism could change within a few years and how the first experimental author and team should be handled; I depend on condensed-matter colleagues.
Whether the source-level IceCube evidence strengthens past 5 sigma soon enough to change my view of B032.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I report no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, or any other credited person on the shortlist. My field is close to B032 and B057, which I treated as a possible taste bias in my opening and have partly corrected by moving to B042. I note Kroll's disclosure of a year in Hall's laboratory and, as chair, consider it not to require recusal on B042.
